topic: Day 2 · Potassium — Hyper- and Hypokalaemia Emergencies
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: Acute physician who runs the resus-room potassium drill and insists that every trainee can recite 'stabilise, shift, remove' — and check the magnesium — before they touch the calcium.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

The crash bleep goes off. A 62-year-old man with diabetic nephropathy on ramipril, spironolactone and — added last week for a UTI — trimethoprim, is found bradycardic and clammy. The monitor shows a slow, broad, bizarre rhythm with towering T waves. The venous gas flashes up: K⁺ 7.8 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 16, creatinine 340. This is a potassium emergency, and you have minutes. The order of your next three drugs — stabilise the myocardium, shift the potassium, then remove it — is the difference between a walk-out and a cardiac arrest. This session drills both ends of the potassium axis, because hypokalaemia kills just as surely, and the two share a hidden puppet-master: magnesium.

1 · ⚡ Why potassium is a cardiac poison at both ends

98% of body potassium is intracellular. The steep gradient across the cell membrane (~140 inside vs ~4 outside) sets the resting membrane potential of every excitable cell. The serum potassium — the tiny 2% we measure — is what governs cardiac conduction, and small changes have huge effects.

  • Hyperkalaemia raises the resting potential (less negative), initially making cells more excitable, then inactivating sodium channels so the cell can't depolarise — conduction slows, the myocardium becomes sluggish and unexcitable → asystole/VF.
  • Hypokalaemia hyperpolarises and delays repolarisation, prolonging the QT/creating U waves and predisposing to re-entrant and torsades-type arrhythmias.
Potassium is the number you never ignore. Both too high and too low stop the heart — hyperkalaemia by paralysing conduction, hypokalaemia by destabilising repolarisation.

2 · 🔺 Hyperkalaemia — mechanism: shift vs total-body excess

Serum potassium rises for two mechanistically distinct reasons, and treatment depends on which:

MechanismCausesTotal body K⁺
Transcellular shift (K⁺ moves OUT of cells)Metabolic acidosis, insulin deficiency/hyperglycaemia (DKA), tissue breakdown (rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, haemolysis), β-blockers, digoxin toxicity, suxamethoniumOften normal — K⁺ is just redistributed
Reduced excretion / total-body excessAKI/CKD (the big one), hypoaldosteronism/Addison's, type-4 RTA, drugs (see below)High
Spurious (pseudohyperkalaemia)Haemolysed sample, tight tourniquet/fist-clenching, delayed processing, marked thrombocytosis/leucocytosisNormal — repeat before treating

The drug list every prescriber must know

  • RAAS inhibitors — ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and MRAs (spironolactone, eplerenone) reduce aldosterone → potassium retention.
  • Trimethoprim (and its combination co-trimoxazole) — blocks the distal epithelial sodium channel like amiloride → hyperkalaemia, especially in renal impairment. Exactly our index patient's added drug.
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride), NSAIDs, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, ciclosporin), heparin, potassium supplements/salt substitutes.
💡 The classic hyperkalaemia recipe

CKD + ACE-inhibitor/ARB + spironolactone + a new course of trimethoprim (or an NSAID) in a patient who then gets a diarrhoeal illness and mild AKI. Each element alone is tolerated; stacked together on a shrinking GFR they produce the 7.8 on the gas. When you add a drug that raises potassium, review the ones already on board.

⚠️ Always exclude pseudohyperkalaemia — but never delay treatment in a sick patient

A haemolysed or clenched-fist sample can read falsely high. If the patient is well with no ECG changes and no reason to be hyperkalaemic, repeat the sample. But if there are ECG changes or the clinical context fits, treat first — a real 7.8 does not wait for a confirmatory venepuncture.

3 · 📉 The ECG evolution — the clock you are racing

ECG change, not the absolute number, drives the urgency — though changes can be absent even at K⁺ >7, so never rely on a normal ECG to reassure you. The classic progression as potassium climbs:

StageECG findingRough K⁺
1Tall, tented, peaked T waves; shortened QT~5.5–6.5
2Flattened/absent P waves; PR prolongation~6.5–7.5
3Widening QRS; conduction blocks~7–8
4Sine wave (QRS merges with T)>8
5VF / asystole / PEA arrestterminal
Peaked T → flat P → wide QRS → sine wave → arrest. Any ECG change beyond peaked T waves is a call for immediate myocardial protection with calcium.

4 · 🚑 Emergency management — stabilise, shift, remove

Three sequential goals, in this order. This is the ladder you recite at 3am (aligned with UK Renal Association / Resuscitation Council guidance):

① STABILISE the myocardium — calcium

  • 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over ~5–10 min (or 10 mL 10% calcium chloride via central access — 3× the elemental calcium, more irritant/sclerosant, reserved for peri-arrest/central line).
  • Give it for any ECG changes (beyond isolated peaked T) or K⁺ ≥6.5 with ECG changes. Onset 1–3 min; lasts only 30–60 min — repeat if ECG doesn't improve or recurs.
  • Calcium does nothing to the potassium level — it raises the threshold potential, restoring the gap between resting and threshold, and buys time. It does not shift or remove potassium.
⚠️ Calcium and digoxin

Traditional teaching cautions against rapid IV calcium in suspected digoxin toxicity (fear of 'stone heart' from calcium-loaded, digoxin-poisoned myocardium). In genuine digoxin-toxic hyperkalaemia the definitive treatment is digoxin-specific antibody fragments (DigiFab). If calcium is needed, give it cautiously/slowly — but do not let dogma cause a preventable arrest; contemporary evidence suggests the risk was overstated.

② SHIFT potassium into cells — insulin-dextrose + salbutamol

  • 10 units soluble insulin (Actrapid) in 25 g glucose (e.g. 250 mL 10% dextrose) IV over 15–30 min. Onset ~15 min, lasts 4–6h, lowers K⁺ by ~0.6–1.2 mmol/L.
  • Monitor blood glucose hourly for at least 6 hours — delayed hypoglycaemia is the commonest iatrogenic complication; give additional dextrose infusion if pre-treatment glucose is low-normal.
  • Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg — β2-agonist drives K⁺ intracellularly; additive to insulin, lowers K⁺ by a further ~0.5–1. Use with care in ischaemic heart disease/tachyarrhythmia. Not reliable as sole therapy (some patients are resistant).
  • Sodium bicarbonate is NOT recommended as a routine shifting agent in acute hyperkalaemia (weak/slow effect); reserve for the profoundly acidotic per specialist advice.

③ REMOVE potassium from the body — the only definitive step

  • Haemodialysis — the definitive treatment, especially in established renal failure, oligo-anuria, or refractory/severe hyperkalaemia. Call renal early.
  • Loop diuretics ± fluid — increase renal excretion if the patient still makes urine and is not volume-depleted.
  • Gut binders — the modern ones: patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC / lokelma) bind potassium in the gut. SZC acts within ~1 hour and is useful acutely as well as chronically; both are far better tolerated than the old resin.
🎯 The demoted role of resonium (calcium/sodium polystyrene sulfonate)

Old-fashioned calcium resonium is slow (hours to days), of doubtful efficacy in the acute setting, unpalatable, and associated with intestinal necrosis (especially with sorbitol and post-operatively). It should not be relied upon to treat acute hyperkalaemia. The newer binders patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate have largely superseded it, and importantly they may allow patients to stay on prognostically important RAAS inhibitors rather than stopping them.

💡 One-line ladder

C BIG K Drop: Calcium (protect) → Beta-agonist + Insulin-Glucose (shift) → K removal by binders/diuretics/Dialysis. And always: stop the offending drugs and treat the cause (AKI, acidosis).

6 · 🔻 Hypokalaemia — causes by mechanism

Mirror the hyperkalaemia logic: potassium is either lost (gut or kidney), shifted in, or intake is inadequate.

MechanismCauses
GI lossDiarrhoea, vomiting/NG suction (via renal loss + alkalosis), laxative abuse, fistulae, villous adenoma
Renal lossLoop & thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism (Conn's), Cushing's, liquorice, Bartter/Gitelman, renal tubular acidosis types 1 & 2, hypomagnesaemia
Transcellular shift (K⁺ into cells)Insulin (esp. DKA treatment), β2-agonists, alkalosis, refeeding, thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, catecholamine surge
Inadequate intakeStarvation, anorexia, alcoholism

ECG of hypokalaemia

  • U waves (extra deflection after the T), T-wave flattening/inversion, ST depression, prolonged QT (really QU) → risk of torsades de pointes and, in digoxin-treated patients, digoxin toxicity (hypokalaemia potentiates digoxin).
Hyperkalaemia peaks the T; hypokalaemia flattens the T and raises a U. Both prolong the danger and both can end in a fatal arrhythmia.

7 · 🧲 The magnesium connection — the hidden puppet-master

Here is the pearl that fixes 'refractory' hypokalaemia: hypomagnesaemia drives renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalaemia impossible to correct until the magnesium is replaced. Low intracellular magnesium releases the inhibition on the ROMK potassium channel in the distal nephron, so the kidney leaks potassium no matter how much you give.

⚠️ You cannot fix the potassium until you fix the magnesium

The classic scenario: an alcoholic or diuretic-using patient whose K⁺ won't budge despite bags of replacement. Check — and replace — the magnesium. The same low magnesium is often silently driving refractory hypocalcaemia and arrhythmia (see session 12). 'Always fix the magnesium' is the one-liner that saves the day.

8 · 💉 Hypokalaemia — replacement done safely

  • Mild (3.0–3.5) & asymptomatic: oral potassium (e.g. Sando-K); treat the cause; often just stop the diuretic.
  • Severe (<2.5), symptomatic, or arrhythmia/ECG changes: IV potassium chloride. Peripheral line: maximum 10 mmol/hour (higher concentrations sclerose veins and are painful). Central line with continuous cardiac monitoring: up to 20 mmol/hour in critical care.
  • Use pre-mixed bags (e.g. 40 mmol KCl in 1 L) — never add strong potassium to a bag on the ward; concentrated KCl boluses cause fatal arrests. Recheck potassium regularly.
  • Always give magnesium alongside if there is any suggestion of depletion, or replacement fails.
🎯 The rough replacement rule of thumb

Serum potassium falls ~0.3 mmol/L for roughly every 100 mmol total-body deficit — so a patient at 2.5 may be 200–400 mmol depleted. This is why hypokalaemia is corrected over hours-to-days, not minutes, and why you keep rechecking rather than assuming one bag fixes it.

☠️ M&M — the refractory potassium that arrested on the ward

A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, on furosemide and spironolactone for ascites, was admitted with diarrhoea. His potassium was 2.4. The house officer prescribed 40 mmol KCl bags and, over the day, ran in 120 mmol — yet the repeat potassium was still 2.5, and he then had a run of torsades and arrested. What was missed: his magnesium was 0.4 mmol/L. Profound hypomagnesaemia was driving relentless renal potassium wasting, so every bag of potassium was being urinated away, and the low magnesium itself was pro-arrhythmic and prolonging his QT. Lessons: (1) refractory hypokalaemia is hypomagnesaemia until proven otherwise — check and replace magnesium first/alongside; (2) an alcoholic on loop + potassium-sparing diuretics with diarrhoea is a magnesium-and-potassium disaster; (3) torsades in this setting is treated with IV magnesium sulfate regardless of the level. They chased the potassium number and never looked at the cation that controlled it.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Hyperkalaemia mechanism = shift vs total-body excess vs spurious — check for haemolysis, but treat a real high potassium immediately.
  2. ECG evolution: peaked T → flat P/wide QRS → sine wave → arrest; any change beyond peaked T demands calcium now.
  3. Emergency ladder: STABILISE (calcium gluconate 10 mL 10%, repeat, protects only) → SHIFT (insulin-dextrose + salbutamol, monitor glucose 6h) → REMOVE (dialysis, loop diuretic, SZC/patiromer).
  4. Resonium is demoted — slow, ineffective acutely, risks bowel necrosis; use patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate.
  5. Stop the culprit drugs — RAAS inhibitors, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAIDs — and treat the AKI/acidosis.
  6. Hypokalaemia: GI/renal loss or shift; U waves and torsades risk; replace IV no faster than 10 mmol/h peripherally (20 central, monitored).
  7. Always fix the magnesium — hypomagnesaemia causes refractory hypokalaemia and pro-arrhythmia; you cannot correct the potassium until the magnesium is replaced.

moderatorQs.q: A patient has K⁺ 7.2 with wide QRS complexes. Rank your first three interventions and say what each actually does.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The order is stabilise, shift, remove. First, calcium — 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV over 5–10 minutes (repeat if the ECG doesn't improve or recurs); it raises the threshold potential to protect the myocardium and buys 30–60 minutes but does nothing to the potassium level. Second, shift — 10 units of soluble insulin in 25 g of glucose IV, plus 10–20 mg nebulised salbutamol, driving potassium intracellularly and dropping it by ~1–1.5 mmol/L over 15–30 minutes (monitor glucose hourly for 6 hours for delayed hypoglycaemia). Third, remove — the only definitive step: loop diuretic if still passing urine, a modern binder (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate acts within an hour), and haemodialysis, which I'd arrange early given his renal failure. Alongside all of this: stop the ACE-inhibitor/spironolactone/trimethoprim and treat the underlying AKI.

moderatorQs.q: Why has calcium/sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) fallen out of favour for acute hyperkalaemia, and what has replaced it?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because it doesn't do the job and it can harm. Resonium is slow (hours to days), of doubtful efficacy in the acute setting, unpalatable, and — particularly with sorbitol, in post-operative or constipated patients — has been associated with intestinal necrosis. So it should not be relied upon to treat an acute hyperkalaemic emergency. It has largely been superseded by two newer gut binders: patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC), which are better tolerated and more effective; SZC in particular acts within about an hour. A valuable secondary benefit is that these agents can control chronic hyperkalaemia well enough to let patients remain on prognostically important RAAS inhibitors rather than stopping them.

moderatorQs.q: You've given three bags of potassium to a patient stuck at K⁺ 2.4 and it won't rise. What is the likely explanation and what do you do?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is refractory hypokalaemia driven by hypomagnesaemia until proven otherwise. Low intracellular magnesium releases the inhibition on the ROMK channel in the distal nephron, so the kidney wastes potassium faster than you can replace it — every bag is being urinated away. The low magnesium is also independently pro-arrhythmic and QT-prolonging. So I would check and replace the magnesium (IV magnesium sulfate), continue potassium replacement, and recheck both. The rule is simple: you cannot correct the potassium until you have corrected the magnesium — and if this patient develops torsades, IV magnesium is the treatment regardless of the measured level.

audienceQs.q: After I give insulin-dextrose for hyperkalaemia, what's the main thing I need to watch for?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Delayed hypoglycaemia — it's the commonest iatrogenic complication of treating hyperkalaemia. The insulin outlasts the glucose you gave with it, so blood sugar can crash an hour or more later. Check the capillary glucose hourly for at least 6 hours after the dose. If the patient's pre-treatment glucose was low-normal (say <7 mmol/L), run an additional 10% dextrose infusion prophylactically. Also remember the insulin-dextrose only shifts potassium into cells for 4–6 hours — the potassium will drift back up unless you have also removed it (binder, diuretic or dialysis) and treated the cause, so recheck the potassium too.

audienceQs.q: A CKD patient on ramipril and spironolactone needs trimethoprim for a UTI. What should I recommend?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Flag this as a high-risk hyperkalaemia combination. Trimethoprim blocks the distal epithelial sodium channel like amiloride and raises potassium, and it's being stacked on two RAAS-acting drugs in a patient with reduced renal reserve. I'd recommend either choosing an alternative antibiotic guided by sensitivities (e.g. nitrofurantoin if eGFR permits, or another agent) or, if trimethoprim is really needed, checking U&Es before and a few days into treatment, considering temporarily holding the spironolactone, counselling on salt-substitute avoidance, and ensuring the patient isn't also on an NSAID. The principle: whenever you add a potassium-raising drug, review the ones already on board.

audienceQs.q: How fast can I safely replace potassium IV in a critically ill patient at 2.3?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Via a peripheral line the ceiling is 10 mmol/hour — higher concentrations are painful and sclerose veins. In critical care with a central line and continuous cardiac monitoring you can go up to 20 mmol/hour for severe, symptomatic hypokalaemia, rechecking the potassium frequently (e.g. 1–2 hourly). Always use pre-mixed bags — never add concentrated KCl to a bag yourself, as bolus potassium causes fatal arrests. Crucially, at 2.3 the total-body deficit is large (roughly 100 mmol per 0.3 mmol/L drop), so this is a job for hours, not minutes, and I'd replace magnesium alongside or the potassium simply won't hold.
